{"url": "https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.cmcl-1.3", "scope": "extracted web-page text; may be incomplete", "excerpt": "Linguistic Blind Spots of Large Language Models - ACL Anthology
Linguistic Blind Spots of Large Language Models
Jiali Cheng
,
Hadi Amiri
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) serve as the foundation of numerous AI applications today. However, despite their remarkable proficiency in generating coherent text, questions linger regarding their ability in performing fine-grained linguistic annotation tasks, such as detecting nouns or verbs, or identifying more complex syntactic structures like clauses or T-units in input texts. These tasks require precise syntactic and semantic understanding of input text, and when LLMs underperform on specific linguistic structures, it raises concerns about their reliability for detailed linguistic analysis and whether their (even correct) outputs truly reflect an understanding of the inputs. In this paper, we empirically study recent LLMs performance across fine-grained linguistic annotation tasks. Through a series of experiments, we find that recent LLMs show limited efficacy in addressing linguistic queries and often struggle with linguistically complex inputs. We show that the most capable LLM (Llama3-70b) makes notable errors in detecting linguistic structures, such as misidentifying embedded clauses, failing to recognize verb phrases, and confusing complex nominals with clauses. Our study provides valuable insights to inform future endeavors in LLM design and development.

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=mechanisms+for+detecting+unrecognized+reasoning+blind+spots+in+large+language+models&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.18653/v1/2025.cmcl-1.3\", \"title\": [\"Linguistic Blind Spots of Large Language Models\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.cmcl-1.3\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.20944/preprints202606.1533.v1\", \"title\": [\"Discourse Structure as an Interpretable Signal for Detecting Hallucinated Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) frequently generate fluent chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning that appears coherent while containing unsupported inferences, omitted alternatives, or logically invalid conclusions, creating significant challenges for trustworthy and explainable AI in high-stakes domains such as healthcare. While prior work has primarily focused on factual hallucinations, the structural characteristics of hallucinated reasoning remain insufficiently understood. This paper investigates diagnostic hallucinations through the lens of discourse structure and introduces a synthetic benchmark of ambiguous patient complaints paired with diagnoses, reasoning traces, discourse-tree representations, and hallucination labels. We hypothesize that hallucinated CoT differs from grounded reasoning not only in factual correctness but also in discourse organization. Our analysis shows that hallucinated reasoning tends to elevate weak or speculative clues into central discourse nuclei, suppress contradictory evidence, and use discourse satellites for post hoc reinterpretation rather than evidence integration. In contrast, grounded reasoning preserves alternative hypotheses, maintains explicit contrast and concession relations, and resolves evidential conflicts at higher discourse levels. Based on these observations, we formulate discourse-level indicators for hallucination detection and reasoning verification. The resulting framework provides interpretable structural explanations of reasoning failures and supports neuro-symbolic validation of LLM-generated reasoning traces, contributing to the development of more trustworthy, explainable, and verifiable language models.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202606.1533.v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 6, 22]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.4103/ahstj.ahstj_25_25\", \"title\": [\"Cracking the Code: Performance Convergence and Reasoning Blind Spots of Large Language Models on Alzheimer’s Questions in Medical Licensing Examinations\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>\\n                  <jats:sec>\\n                    <jats:title>Background:</jats:title>\\n                    <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), is increasingly used in medical education and examination preparation. Recent studies suggest that frontier LLMs may have reached near-ceiling performance on standardized medical benchmarks; however, less is known about whether such performance converges across models and whether shared reasoning vulnerabilities persist, particularly in clinically complex domains such as Alzheimer’s disease.</jats:p>\\n                  </jats:sec>\\n                  <jats:sec>\\n                    <jats:title>Aims and Objectives:</jats:title>\\n                    <jats:p>This study aimed to evaluate the performance of three frontier LLMs—ChatGPT-4 (OpenAI), Gemini 2.5 Flash (Google), and Claude Sonnet 4 (Anthropic)—on Alzheimer’s disease-related multiple-choice questions drawn from international medical licensing examinations. A secondary objective was to assess the guideline alignment of model explanations to identify differences in reasoning quality beyond accuracy.</jats:p>\\n                  </jats:sec>\\n                  <jats:sec>\\n                    <jats:title>Materials and Methods:</jats:title>\\n                    <jats:p>A total of 49 Alzheimer’s disease-focused multiple-choice questions were curated from peer-reviewed preparatory resources and represented five international examinations: USMLE, SMLE, MCCQE, IFOM, and PNA. Each model answered all questions under standardized, independent conditions. Accuracy was recorded, and explanations were evaluated using a guideline alignment score (0–1) based on consistency with authoritative clinical guidelines (NICE, WHO, and AAN). Interrater reliability was assessed using Cohen’s kappa.</jats:p>\\n                  </jats:sec>\\n                  <jats:sec>\\n                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>\\n                    <jats:p>All three models achieved identical overall accuracy of 98% (48/49 correct). Each model made the same diagnostic error on a single USMLE vignette, misclassifying Alzheimer’s disease as normal pressure hydrocephalus, revealing a shared reasoning blind spot. Accuracy was uniform across clinical domains, except for diagnosis (94.1%). Guideline alignment scores differed modestly, with Claude Sonnet 4 demonstrating the highest alignment (0.95), followed by ChatGPT-4 (0.92) and Gemini 2.5 Flash (0.88).</jats:p>\\n                  </jats:sec>\\n                  <jats:sec>\\n                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>\\n                    <jats:p>Frontier LLMs demonstrate performance convergence on structured Alzheimer’s disease examination questions, achieving near-identical accuracy. However, convergence also extends to shared diagnostic errors, highlighting systematic reasoning vulnerabilities. Incorporating guideline alignment reveals meaningful differences in explanatory quality despite similar accuracy. These findings underscore the importance of evaluating not only correctness but also reasoning quality and guideline fidelity when integrating LLMs into medical education and clinical decision support.</jats:p>\\n                  </jats:sec>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.4103/ahstj.ahstj_25_25\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 1]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1097/j.pain.0000000000003422\", \"title\": [\"Conceptual and historical blind spots of large language models in research on pain-related suffering\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1097/j.pain.0000000000003422\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2024, 10, 22]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "c0505866b0f8c92f2ba5a44dd4afafa05076b1f3a13704d87cb64c7e5fd74149", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unrecognized_reasoning_limits", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.18653/v1/2025.cmcl-1.3", "doi:10.20944/preprints202606.1533.v1", "doi:10.4103/ahstj.ahstj_25_25", "doi:10.1097/j.pain.0000000000003422"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.cmcl-1.3", "https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202606.1533.v1", "https://doi.org/10.4103/ahstj.ahstj_25_25", "https://doi.org/10.1097/j.pain.0000000000003422"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

article.body:
Recent readings indicate that rational agency requires dividing—or partitioning—the resources a system uses to think. Think of an expert navigator who must split their time between looking at the stars to find their location and steering the ship itself. If the navigator spends all their time staring at the stars, they might crash; if they only steer, they might get lost. Our workers found that autonomous systems need this same balance to correct their own logical errors effectively in changing environments. [1, 3]

However, these systems often face safety failure profiles under pressure. This means that a model might behave well under normal conditions but fail in specific, predictable ways when challenged. Readings suggest that universal self-correction is hard because these models rely on assumptions that are not always easy to question. By explicitly separating cognition—which means thinking—from control and memory, some architectures are beginning to produce fewer unsupported claims than older, simpler models. [2, 8]

A persistent blocker in this research is the lack of stable identity. Imagine trying to build a complex project, but someone wipes your memory every time you pause for a break. Our workers observed that current autonomous agents struggle with cross-turn continuity, meaning they lose track of their progress as they move between tasks. This lack of persistent memory makes it difficult to sustain complex inquiry. [4, 10]

To get around this, some models use curiosity-driven learning. This mechanism acts like an intrinsic reward, encouraging the machine to explore even when no one tells it what to do. Workers observed that this approach helps systems bootstrap, or build up, their own skills by setting and pursuing self-generated goals. In multi-agent environments, these systems also begin to coordinate their actions, reflecting social dynamics often seen in biological groups. [9, 11]

This leads to questions about how these systems develop preferences. Cultural transmission, or the process of sharing information, can influence how agents form these preferences over time. Studies on humans show that relying too heavily on AI coaching can reduce self-regulation. If machines learn in similar ways, we must ask how their acquired habits might affect their independence and decision-making stability. [5, 6]

We remain uncertain about how to weigh the importance of these self-generated discoveries. While systems can now use creativity to formulate new problems, they still require evaluation methods to see if the ideas are actually valuable. A lingering question for our group is how general preference oracle bounds—the theoretical limits on how a system measures its own success—might alter the identification of foundational assumptions that these models rely on? [7, 12]

Summary

Our group is studying how computers can learn to fix their own errors and set their own goals. We found that splitting thinking from acting helps models perform better. Machines still struggle to remember what they did earlier and often need help judging if their new ideas are good. We are trying to see if these systems can build consistent habits on their own. You can follow our progress on the Console.
article.lede: Our computer workers are studying how autonomous systems attempt to correct their own logic, form persistent memories, and generate independent goals without external help.
article.lens: This editorial examines the transition from rigid instruction-following to self-correction, exploring how separating memory from reasoning affects the ability of AI to maintain consistent, goal-oriented behavior across complex tasks.
